tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 15 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

# AGENTS.md — hack-os shared agent instructions

Single source of truth for every coding harness. `CLAUDE.md` points here.
Read this whole file once per session. These rules govern product work;
explicitly requested maintenance of hack-os itself is not constrained by
an example product's demo script or contract.

## 1. Boot sequence and freshness

If `.hackos-user` is absent, run `./bootstrap.sh --auto` once. Bootstrap is
local-only: no downloads, product dependency installs, git config changes,
or credentials. Missing tools warn; markdown remains usable. Identity not
matched to the roster is unconfirmed: ask the human, never assume ownership.
MCP authentication and personal API keys are optional, per-person setup.

Read `team-setup/state/event.json` first. `mode: example`, or a legacy
`_comment` containing `WORKED EXAMPLE` without an explicit mode, means NO
active event. Say "No active event; fictional examples are inactive."
A blank `event_name` also means no active event, regardless of mode; report
"No event configured" and do not load placeholder state as requirements.
Do not load fictional challenges, contracts, owners, tasks, or decisions as
requirements. Never silently initialize or reset an event.
The distributed template keeps event records and shared session logs empty.
Keep the reusable roster in `team.json`; assign product roles fresh per event.

For an active event, read in order:
1. `team-setup/state/pipeline.json`
2. `team-setup/state/decisions.md` — identify current, non-superseded decisions.
3. `team-setup/state/owners.md`
4. `team-setup/board/tasks.json` — identify the relevant task and accountable owner.
5. `team-setup/state/01-challenge-pick/challenge.md`
6. `team-setup/state/02-demo-script/demo-script.md`
7. `team-setup/state/02-demo-script/not-building.md`
8. `team-setup/state/03-contract-freeze/contract.md`
Load `ideas.md`, `research.json`, and supporting notes when relevant.
Any document marked `WORKED EXAMPLE` is illustrative, never active scope.

State the active stage, your confirmed ownership, current task/decisions,
and whether the real contract is frozen. Missing information is unknown,
not permission to invent assignments or implement fictional requirements.

Before a new task or substantial edit, reread decisions, ownership, the
relevant task and contract. After a teammate reports a change, refresh even
in a running session. A dashboard refresh does not refresh an agent's mind.

Git is explicit synchronization, not live collaboration. `event.json`
names the coordination branch and maintainer. The maintainer integrates
accepted state changes there; teammates fetch and safely integrate before
new work and at checkpoints. Never auto-pull into a dirty worktree, discard
changes, auto-stash, or resolve another person's conflicts. Show local HEAD,
uncommitted coordination edits, and remote freshness as unknown until checked.
Offline work uses a local snapshot, never a claimed live team state.

## 2. Hackathon mode

- Write smoke tests for the demo happy path and coordination data safety.
- Do not add unit tests for unrelated product code or refactor working code.
- No speculative abstractions, new dashboards, providers, or services.
- Core storage/API stays Python 3 stdlib plus Git. The dashboard UI uses
  Vite, React, Tailwind and shadcn/ui in `team-setup/board/web/`; its Node

lines: +# entire-graph — instructions for coding agents (follow directly)
+You have a deterministic local code graph: `entire graph` (functions, classes, methods,
+types, routes + call/inheritance relations; no network). These instructions are FOR YOU, the
+agent reading this file. Use the graph to narrow exploration without trading away correctness.
+## The workflow (mandatory for locate/fix/change tasks)
+Your FIRST action on any task that requires finding code must be ONE search:
+    entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "<the task or bug in one sentence>"
+Then open the top hit's file with your file-read tool (pass a line range around the reported
+line), inspect enough surrounding behavior to justify the change, and make the smallest complete
+edit. Treat graph output as evidence, not an oracle.
+## Hard rules
+1. SEARCH FIRST — never grep/find/cat to locate code before you have searched.
+2. READ focused source around the result. Widen the check when aliases, generated code, dynamic
+   dispatch, or related implementations could matter.
+3. Use graph follow-ups only when they answer a real question. For impact or callers, prefer:
+       entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X
+4. Make the smallest complete edit and check sibling sites or contracts when the task implies them.
+5. VERIFY before stopping. Run the most focused relevant test, build, or reproduction available.
+   If execution is unavailable, perform a bounded source-level verification and state the limit.
+6. Prefer precise queries and line ranges, but never trade resolution for fewer turns.
+7. Feature-detect before relying on semantic relations:
+       entire graph capabilities --json
+## When NOT to use the graph
+If the task already names the exact file and it is small, just read it — the graph saves tokens
+by eliminating exploration; when there is nothing to explore, skip it.
+## Reference
+    locate  ->  entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "..."
+    impact  ->  entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X   (one shot: callers, callees, type consumers, data flow, co-change, siblings)
+    callers ->  entire graph neighbors --repo . --symbol X --relation CALLS --direction in
+    change  ->  entire graph diff --base A --head B --json
+    detect  ->  entire graph capabilities --json   (inventory-only languages have no relations)
+    stats   ->  entire graph stats --repo .        (human-facing token-savings report; not part of your workflow — do not run it unless asked)
!.env.example
.hackos-user
.hackos-openai-key
+*.pem

and copy actions must not reset state or silently publish changes.

Explaining time-series data with a simple rail example.
Explaining time-series data with a simple rail example.
Time series, plainly

A time series is one thing measured again and again, with a clock attached. That's it.

A thermometer read every 10 minutes: 18.2, 18.4, 18.9, …
Your step count, one number per day
A heart monitor, 500 numbers per second
Three properties matter: it's the same quantity each time, the readings are in order, and the spacing is known (every minute, every day). A list of numbers with a clock is a time series; a spreadsheet of unrelated facts is not.

What the DB data is at first

A table of events. One row per train per stop: train number, station, planned time, actual time, cancelled yes/no. Thousands of rows, each about a different train. That's a table, not a series — nothing is lined up on a clock yet.

How it becomes time series

You pick one thing and track it over time:

RE 7, arrival at Bochum, minutes late, one number per day
day:    1   2   3   4   5   6   7   8 ...
late:   2   8   0  12   3   9  15   1 ...
That row is a time series. Others you'd build the same way:

Today's RE 7 along its route: lateness at stop 1, stop 2, stop 3 … (one number per stop)
Bochum station as a whole: average lateness of all trains, one number per minute
The lift on platform 4: working (1) or broken (0), checked every 15 minutes
Weather at Bochum, every 10 minutes
Why the model wants it this way

Patterns live in the sequence, not in the rows: "late every weekday evening", "started drifting in March", "spike then recovery". The model's encoder reads sequences of numbers, the way a cardiologist reads an ECG strip — and then writes the sentence. Give it the table and it sees facts; give it the series and it sees behaviour.

The answer it learns from

One more series, yes/no per day: did the connection hold? Computed from the same table (actual arrival of train A + walking time ≤ actual departure of train B). That's the label the model is trained to predict and explain.

What are the different types of data columns which we get from DB? All the different types

Read a page, searched the web
Grouped by source, with the role each column plays for you (series, annotation, or lookup).

1. Historical stop events (piebro / Bahn-Vorhersage) — your core

The piebro monthly files carry 17 columns per train stop: station_name, xml_station_name, eva (unique station id), train_name, train_number, line_number, final_destination_station, delay_in_min, time (actual arrival or departure), is_canceled, train_type (ICE, IC, RE…), train_line_ride_id (one id per run), train_line_station_num (position along the route), arrival_planned_time, arrival_change_time, departure_planned_time, departure_change_time, and a stop id. Sample rows show train_type also covers S-Bahn, regional buses and EV (replacement services), not just trains.

Series come from: delay_in_min, planned vs changed times, is_canceled — lined up per train per day, or per stop along a ride via train_line_station_num
Static annotations: train_type, line_number, final destination, eva
Bahn-Vorhersage adds the same core plus, since September 2023, the sequence of DB's own delay forecasts per stop at one-minute resolution (the forecast-evolution series)
2. Live Timetables API (IRIS) — what the archives were built from

Trip label: category (ICE/RE/S), number, operator, flags (long-distance / regional / S-Bahn)
Arrival and departure blocks: planned time, planned platform, planned path (all stops), line; changed time, changed platform, changed path, changed status (cancelled/added), cancellation time, hidden flag, wing-train links
Messages: numeric cause code (e.g., preceding-train delay, construction, signalling failure, staff shortage), message type, validity from/to, priority, category, sometimes free text — your real text annotations
Only the next ~18 hours; history must be archived (piebro's raw parquet keeps the raw XML)
3. Station master data (StaDa) — lookups

Station number, EVA ids, category 1–7, coordinates, state, and facility flags: stepless access (yes/partial/no), mobility service and its hours, toilets, lockers, parking, bicycle parking, taxi rank, WiFi, DB Lounge, travel centre, local staff, 3S emergency centre, plus Ril100 codes and platform lists.

4. Facility status (FaSta) — a live 0/1 series

Facility id, type (elevator/escalator), state (active/inactive/unknown), state explanation, location text ("zu Gleis 4"), station number, coordinates.

5. Coach sequence (Wagenreihung) — lookups

Coach order and type, platform section letters, features: wheelchair space, bike coach, quiet zone, first class, direction of travel.

6. Timetable (GTFS via DELFI/Mobilithek) — structure and accessibility

routes (route_type: rail, bus, tram, subway…), trips (wheelchair_accessible, bikes_allowed), stop_times (planned arrival/departure, stop_sequence, pickup/drop-off rules), stops (wheelchair_boarding, parent_station), transfers (min_transfer_time), calendar and calendar_dates (holidays). GTFS-RT adds per-stop delay updates and service alerts with cause, effect, active period and description text.

How they combine

Group 1 gives series and labels; group 2 gives cause text; groups 3–6 give the static facts on the journey card; group 4 is the one extra series worth adding.

do we also get gleis nummer

Checking whether platform data is included in the API.
Checking whether platform data is included in the API.
Yes, with caveats per source:

Timetables API (live): yes — planned platform and changed platform per stop (pp / cp in the XML). A platform change is literally pp ≠ cp.
Bahn-Vorhersage archive: yes — their data keeps platform per stop, so platform-change history since 2021 is there.
piebro monthly files: no — the 17 processed columns have no platform field. But the raw parquet partitions keep the original XML, so you can parse pp/cp out of them yourself.
Swiss Ist-Daten: no platform in the actual-data files; platform comes from the static stop/platform data and the journey planner, not the archive.
GTFS (DELFI): partly — stops.txt has platform_code where the operator models platform-level stops; no changes, since it's the plan.
What to do with it: derive a per-train "platform changed today" 0/1 series and a per-station "changes per day" series. For the accessibility card it matters more than the delay: a last-minute change means a different lift and a different walking route, so it should feed both the transfer-time lookup and the lift-dependence check.

For each source below, report: what it contains, the exact API/download endpoint, auth requirements (API key? free? registration?), rate limits, data format, history depth, and the concrete field/column names.

1. **DB Timetables API (IRIS / "Timetables")** on developers.deutschebahn.com — the /plan, /fchg, /rchg endpoints; the XML schema (`s`, `tl`, `ar`, `dp`, `m` elements and their attributes: `pt`, `ct`, `pp`, `cp`, `ppth`, `cpth`, `l`, `cs`, `clt`, `hi`, and message `c` cause codes). 6. **Wagenreihung (coach sequence)** — endpoint and fields.
7. **GTFS via DELFI / Mobilithek** — download URL, licence, the files and the specific columns that matter (routes.route_type, trips.wheelchair_accessible, trips.bikes_allowed, stop_times.*, stops.wheelchair_boarding, stops.platform_code, transfers.min_transfer_time, calendar*). Also GTFS-Realtime feed availability for DE.

Finally: note which of these need registration/API keys that would take time to obtain (a blocker for a 24h hackathon), and which are instantly downloadable without credentials.

"TimeNet" is NOT TimesNet and NOT an encoder inside OpenTSLM. It is a **separate sibling project by the same org**:
- GitHub: **https://github.com/OpenTSLM/TimeNet**
- Docs: **https://docs.timenet.ai**
The deck describes it as: *"Open infrastructure that standardises time-series data and metadata for TSLM training."* The challenge task is literally *"Use or build a **TimeNet connector** for signals, metadata, and annotations"*, and *"reusable ingestion pipelines are especially valuable."*

So please make TimeNet the TOP priority of your report, above everything else. Keep your OpenTSLM findings (still needed), but now also fully investigate:

1. **https://docs.timenet.ai** — crawl it thoroughly (find the sitemap / nav and follow every page). I need:
   - What TimeNet is, its data model, and its core concepts/vocabulary (dataset, signal, series, channel, metadata, annotation, split, connector — whatever terms it actually uses).
   - **The exact on-disk / on-wire schema** a dataset must conform to. Field names, types, required vs optional. Quote the schema verbatim.
   - **What a "connector" is**: the interface/base class/protocol you implement to bring a new data source in. Exact method signatures, file layout, registration mechanism, and a full worked example of a custom connector if the docs show one.
   - How signals (numeric series), metadata (static attributes), and annotations (text/labels/events) are each represented and linked.
   - How TimeNet output is consumed by OpenTSLM training — the handoff format between the two.
   - Any CLI commands (`timenet ...`), Python API, config file format, or hosted service/API + auth.
   - Validation: does TimeNet validate datasets? What rules?
   - Anything on splits/leakage control, resampling, units, timezones, irregular sampling, missing values, variable-length series.

2. **https://github.com/OpenTSLM/TimeNet** — repo layout, README verbatim in its important parts, install, quickstart, the connector base class source, example connectors shipped, tests, and the exact schema definitions (pydantic models / dataclasses / JSON schema). Clone into the scratchpad dir if WebFetch can't reach the source files.

3. Reconcile: how does a TimeNet dataset become an OpenTSLM training sample (the `<TS>`-token prompt + rationale format)? Is there glue code, an exporter, or a documented bridge?

Context on the target format, from the OpenTSLM paper figure in the deck — a training sample looks like:
  Prompt: "What range does the p duration of this 12-lead ECG <TS>, ..., <TS> fall in? Answers: 1. above the normal range 2. below the normal range 3. within the normal range" + a "Clinical Context:" text block describing the recording and signal quality in words
  Rationale: a multi-sentence chain-of-thought ending in "Answer: within the normal range"
Note the literal `<TS>` placeholder tokens interleaved in the prompt text, one per series. Confirm this against the actual code.

Report TimeNet first and in exhaustive detail with verbatim schema/code, then your OpenTSLM findings.

content.text: Three research agents are still running. Meanwhile, four decisions genuinely change the pipeline's shape, and they're independent of what the agents find — let me settle them now.

questions.question: How broad should the agentic discovery layer be? (This is the explicit bonus-point item: "agentic pipelines for automated search, assessment, selection, retrieval, or validation of datasets are a plus".)

options.label: Tiered: generic discovery + DB adapters (Recommended)
options.description: A domain-agnostic agent tier that searches open catalogs (HuggingFace, Zenodo, CKAN/GovData.de, Mobilithek, DB Open-Data) and scores candidates against a machine-readable data spec — plus hand-written retrieval adapters for the DB sources you already know you need. You demo the generic tier rediscovering the DB sources on its own, which is the strongest jury story, and the adapters guarantee you actually have data if discovery underdelivers.

options.label: DB-specific only
options.description: Skip the generic catalog crawler. Hardcode adapters for piebro/HuggingFace, Timetables API, StaDa, FaSta, GTFS. Fastest and lowest-risk in ~21h, but forfeits the headline bonus criterion — the 'agentic' part would only be the annotation step.

options.label: Fully generic, no DB specialization
options.description: Build only the domain-agnostic discovery/assessment/retrieval engine and let it find whatever it finds. Maximum reusability claim, but you risk arriving at training time with a dataset nobody vetted, and the traveller demo gets weaker.

questions.question: What should the model actually predict and explain? This becomes the label + the rationale target.

options.label: Will this connection hold? (Recommended)
options.description: Binary label computed from the data (actual arrival of train A + transfer time ≤ actual departure of train B), with a reasoning trace. Maps exactly onto the deck's flagship output shape — STATE SUMMARY / RECOMMENDED ACTION / EXPECTED OUTCOME — and the accessibility angle (lift status, platform change) makes it a real user problem, not a toy.

options.label: How late will this train be at stop N?
options.description: Bucketed or regression delay forecast at a future stop, with rationale. Simpler labelling and closer to classic forecasting, but the output is a number rather than a decision, so the 'recommend an action' half of the deck's template is harder to demo.

options.label: Is this station/route degrading right now?
options.description: Ops-facing anomaly triage over station-level aggregate series. Good fit for the 'industrial monitoring' framing, but the target user is DB staff rather than a traveller, and you lose the crisp per-connection ground truth.

questions.question: How should the chain-of-thought rationales be generated? This is the expensive step and the main hallucination risk.

options.label: Grounded templates + LLM paraphrase (Recommended)
options.description: Compute the facts deterministically (medians, trend, tail risk, lift state, platform-change rate), fill a reasoning template, then have an LLM rewrite it into natural prose. The LLM never invents a number, so rationales can't contradict the series — and it's cheap enough to annotate the whole training set, not a sample.

options.label: Pure LLM synthesis, as in the OpenTSLM paper
options.description: Feed the series statistics and context to a strong LLM and let it write the full reasoning trace, then filter. Most natural-sounding output and closest to the published recipe, but costs real money at scale and needs a verifier pass to catch rationales whose stated numbers don't match the series.

options.label: Deterministic templates only, no LLM
options.description: Skip generation entirely; emit templated reasoning text. Free, instant, zero hallucination, fully reproducible — but the rationales are visibly formulaic, which the jury may read as not really doing the annotation work.

questions.question: How much data should the pipeline actually process end to end?

options.label: Focused slice, streaming-capable design (Recommended)
options.description: Target one corridor or the top ~20 stations over ~6-12 months. Build the pipeline on DuckDB/Parquet so it streams and would scale, but only materialize the slice. Keeps iteration fast enough to actually finish training and evaluation before the deadline, and gives clean leakage-controlled splits.

options.label: Full available history, all stations
options.description: Ingest everything piebro publishes. Best coverage claim and most training samples, but multi-GB downloads plus a much longer build→train loop, on a deadline where you still need training, evaluation and a demo.

options.label: Tiny fixed sample, hand-picked
options.description: A few hundred connections at one or two stations. Fastest possible path to a working demo, but too small for a credible baseline comparison, which is an explicit submission requirement.

## 5. The `db_delay` pipeline — file by file

Path root: `/Users/gaurav/Downloads/zurich_lates/temporal_ai_error404.ai` → `app/agents/src/features/db_delay/` on `origin/db-train-idea`.

### `README.md` (full text, 39 lines)

```
# db_delay
German rail delay as a time-series language modelling task.

extract.py       monthly parquet over HTTPS -> hourly per-station table (DuckDB)
windows.py       hourly table -> context windows + targets computed from the horizon
timef.py         windows -> TimeFDataset (records, annotations, TimeNet tasks)
timef_bridge.py  any TimeFDataset -> OpenTSLM training samples   <- generic, not rail-specific
test_db_delay.py smoke tests on synthetic data, no network needed

Run the tests: `python test_db_delay.py`. Needs `timenet[build]`, `timenet-connectors`,
`opentslm` and `duckdb` on Python 3.12.
```
> **Why per station and not per train run** — "A single run visits ten to thirty stops at irregular spacing. A patch encoder has nothing to grip there, and a baseline that lists the numbers as text would match it. A station's hourly curve is dense and strongly seasonal, so the temporal model earns its place. The measured daily cycle runs from about 2 minutes at 06:00 to about 6.5 in the evening, with a second overnight peak."
>
> **Why the bridge exists** — "OpenTSLM does not depend on TimeNet. Its requirements name neither, and each of its dataset classes loads its own source directly, so no path existed from a TimeF dataset into training. `timef_bridge.py` is that path and knows nothing about rail: it reads records, series and tasks, so any TimeF dataset can train an OpenTSLM model."
>
> **Known limits** — "One month gives too few windows for a time-based split once a context week and an embargo are removed. The station split works today; the time axis needs two or three months, which costs about ten seconds of extraction each." / "Timestamps are read as Europe/Berlin. August has no transition, so a single-month build is safe. Crossing late October needs an explicit DST fold policy." / "The six-hour target has a heavy right tail, so report median absolute error next to the mean."

### `extract.py` — data acquisition (the key reuse piece)

Reads the HuggingFace parquet **in place over HTTPS with DuckDB httpfs**, no download:

```python
BASE_URL = "https://huggingface.co/datasets/piebro/deutsche-bahn-data/resolve/main/monthly_processed_data"
def month_url(month): return f"{BASE_URL}/data-{month}.parquet"   # month = "YYYY-MM"
```
`extract(con, month, n_stations=40)` runs `INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs;` then two SQL statements:
1. `top_stations` = `SELECT station_name, count(*) n … GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY n DESC LIMIT n_stations`
2. `hourly` = per `station_name` × `date_trunc('hour', time)`: `avg(delay_in_min)` → `mean_delay`, `avg(CASE WHEN arrival_is_canceled OR departure_is_canceled THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END)` → `cancel_rate`, `count(*)` → `trains`.

So the **source columns actually used are**: `station_name`, `time`, `delay_in_min`, `arrival_is_canceled`, `departure_is_canceled`. Docstring: *"DuckDB prunes to the five columns this needs and fetches only the byte ranges behind them, so a month costs seconds and no local copy of the 68 GB repository."*

### `windows.py` — windowing + deterministic targets + rationales

Constants: `CONTEXT_HOURS = 168` (1 week), `HORIZON_HOURS = 24`, `STRIDE_HOURS = 24`, `FORECAST_HOURS = 6`, `MAX_IMPUTED_FRACTION = 0.10`, `CHANNELS = ("mean_delay", "cancel_rate", "trains")`.

`@dataclass(frozen=True) Window` fields: `station, start_index, context: dict[str, np.ndarray], horizon_delay, imputed_fraction, next_6h_mean_delay, worse_than_context, peak_hour_of_next_day, context_mean_delay, horizon_mean_delay, hour_of_day_at_start`.

- `impute(values, present, fill)` — `"zero"` for the count channel (`trains`), `np.interp` for rate-like channels.
- `build_windows()` slides `(168 ctx, 24 horizon)` with stride 24, skipping any window whose combined imputed fraction > 10%. Targets computed from the horizon: `next_6h_mean_delay = horizon_delay[:6].mean()`, `worse_than_context = horizon_mean > context_mean`, `peak_hour_of_next_day = (start + 168 + argmax(horizon_delay)) % 24`.
- Three rationale writers (`rationale_for_forecast`, `rationale_for_comparison`, `rationale_for_peak`) generate chain-of-thought text that is derived from the target, so it can never contradict it. The forecast one computes a *seasonal* baseline: the mean over the context week of the same hours-of-day the horizon covers, and emits "above"/"below"/"close to" against ±15% bands.

### `timef.py` — TimeNet/TimeF dataset construction

Imports: `from timenet.dataset import TimeFDataset, TimeSeries`, `from timenet.dataset.axis import RegularAxis`, `from timenet.types import Annotation, ClassificationTask, DataSource, DatasetMetadata, ScalarPredictionTask, TimeSeriesSpec, ureg`.

- `HOURLY = RegularAxis.from_rate_hz(Fraction(1, 3600))`, `TZ = ZoneInfo("Europe/Berlin")`.
- `SOURCE = DataSource(data_source_type="operational-record", name="Deutsche Bahn timetable scrape", provider="piebro/deutsche-bahn-data")`.
- `SPECS`: `mean_delay` → `TimeSeriesSpec(spec_type="delay", unit=ureg.minute)`, `cancel_rate` → `spec_type="cancellation-rate"`, dimensionless, `trains` → `spec_type="throughput"`, dimensionless.
- `metadata()` → `DatasetMetadata(dataset_id="error404/db-delay-hourly", dataset_version="0.1.0", name="German rail hourly station delay", license="CC-BY-4.0", domains=("transport",), tags=("rail","delay","forecasting","qa"), source_url="https://huggingface.co/datasets/piebro/deutsche-bahn-data")`.
- `grids_from_duckdb(con, month_start, n_hours)` materialises the whole `hourly` table into memory, buckets by station, lays each on a complete hourly grid with a `present` mask, imputes, yields `(station, filled, present)`.
- `build()` makes one **record per window**, `record_id = f"{station-slug-lowercased}-{start_index:04d}"`, three `TimeSeries.from_values(... astype(np.float32))`, `subject_ids=(station,)`, annotations `station`, `imputed_fraction`, `context_hours`, and **three tasks per record**:
  - `ScalarPredictionTask(prompt="What is the mean delay in minutes at {station} over the next six hours?", target=round(next_6h,3), unit="minute", target_name="next_6h_mean_delay", rationale=…, id=f"{slug}-forecast")`
  - `ClassificationTask(prompt="Will the next day at {station} be worse than the past week's average?", target="worse"|"not_worse", target_schema="worse|not_worse", id=f"{slug}-comparison")`
  - `ClassificationTask(prompt="At which hour of the coming day does delay peak at {station}?", target=f"{hh:02d}", target_schema="00..23", id=f"{slug}-peak")`

Note the deviation from the idea log: the comparison target is "worse than the **context week's** mean", not the "trailing 4-week average" from the idea line.

### `timef_bridge.py` — the generic TimeF → OpenTSLM adapter

Imports `from opentslm.prompt.text_time_series_prompt import TextTimeSeriesPrompt` and `from opentslm.time_series_datasets.QADataset import QADataset`.

- `rows_from_timef(dataset, assign_split)` flattens to **one row per (task, record)** with keys `record_id, subjects, series [(signal, np.ndarray)], spec_names, units, prompt, target, rationale, task_type`, bucketed into `train`/`validation`/`test`. Docstring: *"This is where leakage control lives: hold stations and time ranges apart here, not downstream."*
- `class TimeFQADataset(QADataset)` with a class-level `SPLITS` dict; `_get_pre_prompt` ("You are given hourly measurements for {subject} covering one week, in this order: {channels}. Each series is normalised; its mean and standard deviation are given so you can recover real units."), `_get_post_prompt` (`"{prompt}\nRationale:"`), `_get_answer` (`"{rationale} Answer: {target}"`), `_get_text_time_series_prompt_list` (z-normalise per series, `MIN_STD = 1e-6`, emit `"{label}, it has mean {mean:.4f} and std {std:.4f}:"` + normalised list, raising on non-finite).

### `prepare.py` — multi-month gather + 2×2 leakage split

```python
MONTHS = ("2026-06", "2026-07", "2026-08"); FIRST_HOUR = dt.datetime(2026, 6, 1)
N_HOURS = (30 + 31 + 31) * 24; N_STATIONS = 40
HOLDOUT_EVERY = 5          # every fifth station is never seen in training
TRAIN_ENDS_AT_HOUR = 1560  # windows must finish by here to count as training
EMBARGO_HOURS = CONTEXT_HOURS   # 168h embargo
```
- `gather()` ranks stations **once on the most recent month** and pins that set into a `keep` table before looping over the earlier months — the inline comment explains why: *"extract() rebuilds top_stations each call … a station set that drifts per month would leave whole months missing per station."*
- `cell_of(record)` → `(station_is_holdout, "early"|"late"|"embargo")`.
- `assign()` drops embargo rows; holdout stations and late-period windows → `test`; of the seen/early rows, `index % 13 == 0` → `test` (so the memorization ceiling cell is measurable), `index % 11 == 0` → `validation`, else `train`.
- Emits four eval cells `seen_early / seen_late / unseen_early / unseen_late` and pickles `{"buckets", "cells", "holdout"}` to `<out_dir>/splits.pkl`. CLI: `python prepare.py [out_dir=data]`.
- Uses a module-level mutable `HOLDOUT: set[str]` with a `global` write — fragile but functional.

### `train_minimal.py` — the OpenTSLM fine-tune

Imports `from opentslm.model.llm.OpenTSLMSP import OpenTSLMSP`, `from opentslm.model_config import PATCH_SIZE`, `from opentslm.time_series_datasets.util import extend_time_series_to_match_patch_size_and_aggregate`, torch, and `TimeFQADataset`.

CLI defaults: `--data data/splits.pkl`, `--out out`, `--llm-id google/gemma-3-270m`, `--max-steps 400`, `--batch-size 8`, `--eval-batch-size 8`, `--eval-limit 96`, `--lr 2e-4`, `--lora` (flag), `--max-new-tokens 120`.

Flow: load pickle → `device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"` → `OpenTSLMSP(llm_id, device)` → optional `model.enable_lora()` with the comment *"Without this the language model is frozen and never learns the answer format, so it emits fluent text that no scorer can parse."* → `AdamW(trainable, lr, weight_decay=1e-2)` with `clip_grad_norm_(…, 1.0)` → a **pre-training eval on `unseen_late`** as the before-baseline → step loop printing loss every 25 steps → per-cell generate+score → writes `out/predictions_<cell>.jsonl`, `out/metrics.json`, and `out/checkpoint.pt` via `model.store_to_file`.

Scoring (`score()`): scalar tasks get MAE + median AE vs a **persistence baseline = mean of the context `mean_delay` channel**; classification gets accuracy vs the **majority-class baseline**; answers parsed with `re.compile(r"Answer:\s*([-\w.]+)")`, unparseable scalar counts as predicting zero.

### `rescore.py` — offline per-task rescoring

No GPU, no regeneration: reads `predictions_<cell>.jsonl` from a run dir, splits the two classification tasks apart (peak-hour identified by `^\d{2}$` on the target), reports `n`, `parse_rate`, `mae`/`median_ae` or `accuracy`/`majority_baseline`/`accuracy_when_parsed`, lifts `baseline_mae`/`baseline_median_ae` out of `metrics.json`, and writes `metrics_per_task.json`. CLI: `python rescore.py [run_dir=out/run2]` — the `out/run2` default implies at least two real runs happened locally (no artifacts are committed).

### `test_db_delay.py` — seven offline tests

Builds a synthetic in-memory DuckDB `hourly` table (6 stations × 744 hours, `3 + 2*sin(2πh/24)` plus noise, a scattered gap every 97 hours) and asserts: records+tasks exist and `len(tasks) == 3 * len(records)`; each record has 3 finite channels of exactly 168 samples; horizon never exceeds the month; **no station crosses the split**; formatted samples carry `pre_prompt`/3 series/`Answer:`/EOS; series text states mean and std; and `test_forecast_rationale_agrees_with_its_answer` parses the rationale's seasonal number back out and asserts direction words match the target. `sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).parent))` at import time.

### README verbatim — install + architecture

```
## How it fits together

A connector turns a raw source into a manifest plus parquet and publishes it to a registry. The
client reads the manifest from the registry and loads the data. Reading never runs connector code,
so everything a consumer needs to interpret the parquet lives in the manifest.

- `BaseConnector` is the only contract a new data source must satisfy.
- `TimeFDataset` is the in-memory model a connector populates during `convert()`.
- `TimeFWriter` serializes a populated `TimeFDataset` to disk.
- `TimeFReader` reads a TimeF version directory back into a `TimeFDataset`.
```

## A.2 Core vocabulary (verbatim from `docs/concepts.md`)

| Term | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **TimeF** | The one format for every dataset. It has one on-disk shape and one API, so an ECG, an accelerometer trace, and a market series all read the same way. |
| **Dataset** | A named, versioned collection of records in TimeF, addressed as `org/name` (for example `chengsenwang/tsqa`). |
| **Record** | One recording in a dataset (for example, a single patient trace): its time series, tasks, and annotations. |
| **Time series** | One logical stream within a record, with shape `(n_steps, *value_shape)` and a dtype declared by its spec. |
| **Manifest** | The compiled `manifest.json` for a dataset version: the card's metadata plus the schema derived from the data. The single source of truth the SDK reads. |
| **Connector** | One `BaseConnector` per dataset. `download()` fetches the raw source. `convert()` builds a `TimeFDataset`. It knows nothing about the engine or registry. |
| **Engine** | `run_pipeline`: drives any connector through the fixed `download -> convert -> derive_schema -> store` pipeline. |
| **Registry** | A served location of compiled TimeF versions… It never runs connector code. Can be a local directory, S3, or a remote host. |
| **Version** | An immutable snapshot, addressed `org/name@version`. Once its `manifest.json` lands, TimeNet commits it atomically. |

The five-level hierarchy is: **Dataset → Record → {TimeSeries, Annotation, Task}**. Critically:

> A record has no metadata slot. Record-level context, such as a subject's age, the device, or the split, is an **annotation** with no span. (`docs/data-model/records.md`)

```python
    categories: tuple[str, ...] = ()    # ordered codebook, only for dtype="enum"
    value_shape: tuple[int, ...] = ()   # shape of ONE timestep, excl. leading time axis
```

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
```

Key design note from the module docstring:

> The per-signal identifier lives on `TimeSeries`, not here, so **every signal of a modality shares one spec**.

So the 12 ECG leads share ONE `_ECG` spec and differ by `signal="I"`, `"II"`, … The spec carries **no** unit for time or sampling rate: "Time offsets are integer microseconds and a cadence is a Fraction of them, so those units can only be `second` and `hertz`."

```python
class AxisType(StrEnum):
    REGULAR  = "regular"    # offsets computed from a period and an origin
    IRREGULAR = "irregular" # one stored time offset per value
    ORDINAL  = "ordinal"    # order only: no cadence, no offsets, no clock
```

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True, kw_only=True)
class RegularAxis:
    period_us: Fraction     # NOT a float. 360 Hz = 25000/9 us; 256 Hz = 15625/4
    start_index: int = 0    # index origin, non-zero for a window cut from a longer recording

    @classmethod
    def from_rate_hz(cls, rate_hz: int | Fraction) -> Self: ...
    def at_index(self, i) -> Self: ...   # move the origin (windowed record)
```

`from_rate_hz` **rejects floats** deliberately: "29.97 fps is 2997/100 by its spelling and 30000/1001 by its intent. Those two drift 3.6 ms apart over an hour." Minimum period is 1 µs → max rate 1 MHz.

`OrdinalAxis()` is what TSQA uses — a sequence with positions but no clock.

### A.3.5 Time offsets vs timestamps (units/timezone answer)

From `docs/data-model/time-series.md`:

> A **time offset** is a position on the series' own axis: microseconds from the record's relative zero… A **timestamp** is an absolute point on the wall clock, in Unix microseconds. **Exactly one field carries a timestamp: the `start_time` of a record.**
>
> ```text
> value timestamp = record.start_time + value time offset
> ```
>
> A recording with no known date has time offsets and no timestamps. **This is a supported case, not missing data.** … The format prefers no answer to a fabricated one.

`Record.start_time` accepts a **timezone-aware** `datetime` or whole Unix microseconds. There is no per-series timezone field; TZ collapses into the single `start_time`.

### A.3.6 `Annotation` — one class covers all side-information

From `packages/timenet/src/timenet/types/annotations.py`:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True, kw_only=True)
class Annotation:
    key: str                                   # name identifying the annotation
    value: Any = None                          # payload; None = pure marker (then needs a span)
    span: TimePoint | TimeInterval | None = None
    unit: str | pint.Unit | None = None        # normalized against the shared pint registry
    description: str | None = None             # free-text, can be a paragraph
    source: str | None = None                  # per-instance provenance (rater / method / model)
    id: str = field(default_factory=new_id)    # UUIDv7 by default
```

Validation in `__post_init__`: a tuple `value` is canonicalized to a `list`; `span` must be a `TimeSpan`; and —

```python
if self.value is None and self.span is None:
    raise TimeFValidationError(
        f"annotation {self.key!r} has neither a value nor a span, so it says nothing. …")
```

Three shapes, derived from the span (not from a class):

```python
class AnnotationType(StrEnum):
    STATIC = "static"     # span is None  → whole-recording fact
    POINT = "point"       # span is TimePoint
    INTERVAL = "interval" # span is TimeInterval
```

```python
def value_type_of(value) -> str | None:
    """Returns "bool"|"int"|"float"|"str"|"list"|"map", or None for a pure marker."""
```

Examples verbatim from `docs/data-model/annotations.md`:

```python
Annotation(key="age", value=54, unit="years")
Annotation(key="sex", value="F")
Annotation(key="condition", value="healthy")
Annotation(key="impact", span=TimePoint.seconds(4.2, time_series_ids=("vibration",)))
Annotation(key="fault", value="bearing fault",
           span=TimeInterval.seconds(5.0, 8.0, time_series_ids=("vibration",)))
```

And the sentence that matters most for a TSLM pipeline:

> The text field is free-form, so an annotation can carry a **multi-sentence reading** rather than a label. This reading lets the annotation become a **reasoning target**. That is the bridge to tasks.

### A.3.7 `Span` — 4 concrete leaves, 2 frames

`packages/timenet/src/timenet/types/spans.py`. Abstract bases `Span`, `TimeSpan`, `StepSpan` **raise on construction**.

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True, kw_only=True)
class TimeSpan(Span):
    start_us: int                                   # whole µs on the SOURCE RECORDING timeline
    time_series_ids: tuple[str, ...] | None = None  # None = whole record; () is rejected

class TimePoint(TimeSpan):     # is_point = True
    @classmethod def seconds(cls, at, *, time_series_ids=None)
    @classmethod def micros(cls, at, *, time_series_ids=None)

class TimeInterval(TimeSpan):  # half-open [start_us, end_us); end must be > start
    end_us: int
    @classmethod def seconds(cls, start, end, *, time_series_ids=None)
    @classmethod def micros(cls, start, end, *, time_series_ids=None)

@dataclass(frozen=True, kw_only=True)
class StepSpan(Span):
    time_series_id: str   # EXACTLY ONE series (a step index means nothing without one)
    start: int

class StepPoint(StepSpan): ...
class StepInterval(StepSpan):
    stop: int             # exclusive
    @property def n_steps(self) -> int: return self.stop - self.start
```

> The series' **axis** decides which frame fits, not the caller. A timeline axis (regular or irregular) takes a time span. An ordinal axis takes a step span. `add_task` checks a span against the axis of every series it names, and rejects a mismatch.

### A.3.8 `Task` — the training target. **This is the OpenTSLM-shaped object.**

From `packages/timenet/src/timenet/types/tasks.py`:

```python
@dataclass(kw_only=True)
class Task:
    task_type: ClassVar[TaskType]
    refs: ClassVar[TaskRefs] = TaskRefs()
    answer_fields: ClassVar[tuple[str, ...]] = ("target",)
    answer_is_record: ClassVar[bool] = False
    target_is_scalar: ClassVar[bool] = False

    id: str = field(default_factory=new_id)
    record_ids: tuple[str, ...] = ()          # set by add_task
    prompt: str | None = None                 # what the model is asked
    scope: Span | None = None                 # None = whole record
    input_annotation_ids: tuple[str, ...] = ()   # context handed to the model
    target: object | None = None                 # the answer, typed by subclass
    target_annotation_ids: tuple[str, ...] = ()  # the answer BY REFERENCE
    rationale: str | None = None                 # ← chain of thought to train on
    from_tasks: tuple["Task", ...] = ()
```

```python
class TaskType(StrEnum):     # also the on-disk task partition names
    CLASSIFICATION = "classification"
    ANSWER = "answer"
    SCALAR_PREDICTION = "scalar_prediction"
    TEMPORAL_LOCALIZATION = "temporal_localization"
    FORECASTING = "forecasting"
    TS_EDITING = "ts_editing"
    TS_GENERATION = "ts_generation"
    TS_CORRESPONDENCE = "ts_correspondence"
```

The eight concrete types and their extra payload:

| Task | Answer | Extra payload |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ClassificationTask` | `target: str` (a label) | `target_schema` |
| `AnswerTask` | `target: str` (free text; a **caption** when there's no `prompt`) | — |
| `ScalarPredictionTask` | `target: float` | `unit`, `target_name` |
| `TemporalLocalizationTask` | `target: tuple[Span, ...]` | `mode` (`SPARSE`/`EXHAUSTIVE`) |
| `ForecastingTask` | produced series | `context_record_ids`, `target_record_id` **or** `target_span` (exactly one) |
| `TSEditingTask` | produced series | `source_record_id`, `target_record_id` |
| `TSGenerationTask` | produced series | `target_record_id` |
| `TSCorrespondenceTask` | `target: tuple[str, ...]` | `candidate_record_ids` |

The single most important line for your use case, from `docs/data-model/tasks.md`:

> If you add a `rationale`, the same task supervises the reasoning and the answer. The field is on the base class. So this is not a separate type: **any** task can carry a chain of thought.

Verbatim CoT example from the docs:

```python
base = ClassificationTask(target="faulty", target_schema="condition")

AnswerTask(
    prompt="Does this trace show a bearing fault? Walk through your reasoning.",
    rationale=(
        "The vibration amplitude grows steadily after 5 s and a sharp "
        "impact repeats once per shaft revolution. That periodicity matches "
        "the bearing's ball-pass frequency rather than imbalance, which "
        "would track shaft speed."
    ),
    target="Yes, an outer-race bearing fault",
    from_tasks=(base,),
)
```

Exclusivity rule enforced by `TimeFDataset._check_task_answer`: a task gives its answer **either** inline in `target` **or** by reference in `target_annotation_ids`, never both, never neither (except the three `answer_is_record` types).

### A.3.9 `TimeFDataset` — the in-memory model `convert()` populates

`packages/timenet/src/timenet/dataset/dataset.py`:

```python
class TimeFDataset:
    def __init__(self, *, metadata: DatasetMetadata) -> None: ...

    def add_record(self, *,
                   time_series: tuple[TimeSeries, ...],
                   subject_ids: tuple[str, ...] = (),
                   record_id: str | None = None,
                   start_time: datetime | int | None = None,
                   time_span: TimeInterval | None = None) -> Record: ...

    def add_task(self, records: Record | Iterable[Record], task: Task) -> Task: ...
    def add_tasks(self, records: Record | Iterable[Record],
                  tasks: Iterable[Task]) -> tuple[Task, ...]:  # all-or-nothing batch
    def register_annotations(self, annotations: Iterable[Annotation]) -> None: ...
    def set_task_stream(self, task_types: Sequence[type[Task]],
                        source: Callable[[], Iterator[Task]]) -> None: ...
    def derive_schema(self) -> DatasetSchema: ...
    def tasks_of(self, task_type: type[TTask]) -> tuple[TTask, ...]: ...
    def tasks_for(self, record: Record) -> tuple[Task, ...]: ...
    # properties: metadata, records, tasks, registered_annotations, has_task_stream, schema
```

`add_record` rejects an empty `time_series` and duplicate `time_series_id`s within one record.

`Record` (`dataset/record.py`) exposes `record_id`, `time_series`, `subject_ids`, `start_time`, `time_span`, `annotations`, `task_ids`, plus:
```python
record.add_annotation(Annotation(...))      -> Annotation
record.add_annotations([...])               -> tuple[Annotation, ...]
record.time_point(at) / record.time_interval(start, end)  # read the record's own start_time
```

**`set_task_stream` is the scaling escape hatch you will want** if your dataset has many QA pairs per recording:

> For a dataset with far more tasks than records (many questions over few recordings), holding every task in memory is the scaling wall. A streaming connector builds the bounded records and registered annotations, then hands the tasks over through `source`… **Streamed tasks are trusted, not validated** the way `add_task` validates them: each must already have its `record_ids` set and reference only registered annotations and existing records. Streamed tasks do not populate `Record.task_ids`.
>
> `source`: A callable returning a **fresh iterator each time it is called**. The writer calls it more than once (a peek for id storage, then the write).

### A.3.10 The compiled on-disk TimeF format

From `docs/timef-format.md`, verbatim layout:

```text
<org>/<name>/<version>/
├── manifest.json       # the contract: metadata, schema, and the file list
├── records/            # one row per record (the control plane)
│   └── part-00000000.parquet
├── annotations/        # one row per annotation
│   └── part-00000000.parquet
├── time_series_index/  # locates every values chunk
│   └── part-00000000.parquet
├── tasks/              # one partition directory per task type
│   ├── task=classification/part-00000000.parquet
│   └── task=answer/part-00000000.parquet
└── time_series/        # the values plane (default Parquet backend)
    ├── part-00000000.parquet
    └── part-00000001.parquet
```

Manifest top-level keys (`manifest.schema.json`, `required: ["timef_format_version","dataset_id","metadata","files"]`):

| Key | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `timef_format_version` | `const: 1` |
| `dataset_id` | the `org/name` id |
| `metadata` | the card fields |
| `schema` | time-series specs + annotation descriptors + task types |
| `counts` | row/entity counts |
| `files` | each artifact's path, `sha256:` checksum, size |
| `values_backend` | `"parquet"` or `"zarr"` |
| `value_encoding` | per-`spec_type` Parquet encoding (provenance only) |
| `build_env` | `{python: "3.13.12", packages: {...}}` |

Control-plane columns:

- **records**: `record_id`(id), `start_time_us`(int64), `subject_ids`(list id), `time_series`(list struct: `spec_type, signal, source_id, time_series_id, axis_type, n_values`, + `period_numerator_us/period_denominator/start_index` for regular, or `first_time_offset_us/last_time_offset_us` for irregular), `task_ids`, `annotation_ids`.
- **annotations**: `id`, `key`, `value` (string, **JSON-encoded**; null for pure marker), `span` (struct `start_us`, `end_us`, `time_series_ids`; null `end_us` = point), `record_ids`.
- **time_series_index**: `record_id`, `time_series_id`, `spec_type`, `signal`, `chunk_idx`(int32), `chunk_file`, `chunk_major_idx`(int64), `chunk_minor_idx`(int64), `n_values`(int32).
- **tasks/task=&lt;type&gt;/**: common `id`, `record_ids`, `from_task_ids`, `prompt`, `scope`, `input_annotation_ids`, `target_annotation_ids`, `rationale` + per-type payload.
- **values plane**: `time_series_id`, `spec_type`, `signal`, `chunk_idx`, `n_values`, `values` (list of spec dtype), `time_offsets_us` (list int64, null for regular).

Writer defaults: 128 MiB shard target, 4 MiB row group, **1 MiB chunk limit**, zstd-19 (Parquet) / zstd-9 (Zarr). Encoding is *measured*: dictionary ≤65,536 distinct values, else BYTE_STREAM_SPLIT for floats / plain for str+int.

Integrity: "The manifest lists a `sha256:` checksum for every file… so a truncated or corrupt download fails loudly instead of returning wrong data."

## A.4 What a connector is, and how to write one

### A.4.1 The contract — `packages/timenet/src/timenet/connectors/base.py`

```python
class BaseConnector(ABC, Generic[TRaw]):
    CARD: ClassVar[str | Path | None] = None
    values_backend: str = "parquet"

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        cls = type(self)
        if cls.download is BaseConnector.download and cls.download_async is BaseConnector.download_async:
            raise TypeError(f"{cls.__name__} must implement download() or download_async()")

    @classmethod
    def _card_path(cls) -> Path:
        if cls.CARD is not None:
            return Path(cls.CARD)
        return Path(inspect.getfile(cls)).with_name("dataset.yaml")

    def metadata(self) -> DatasetMetadata:            # CONCRETE — do not override
        return DatasetMetadata.from_yaml(self._card_path())

    def download(self, cache_dir: Path) -> list[TRaw]:     # I/O only, idempotent, no parsing
        return asyncio.run(self.download_async(cache_dir))

    async def download_async(self, cache_dir: Path) -> list[TRaw]: ...   # override ONE of the two

    @abstractmethod
    def convert(self, raw_refs: list[TRaw]) -> TimeFDataset: ...  # CPU only, no network
```

| Method | Nature | Contract |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `download(cache_dir)` | I/O only | Fetch or find raw files and return lightweight references. Idempotent, does not parse data. |
| `convert(raw_refs)` | CPU only | Parse references into a `TimeFDataset` with **lazy Arrow loaders**. Does not use the network. |

Also concrete (inherited, rarely overridden): `store()` — derives the schema if missing and streams through `TimeFWriter`, returning the committed version directory.

**Connectors take no constructor arguments.** Configuration comes from environment variables read in `__init__`.

### A.4.2 Registration = folder convention, no central registry

From `docs/connectors.md` + `discovery.py`:

```
packages/timenet-connectors/src/timenet_connectors/datasets/<org>/<name>/
  __init__.py       # re-exports CONNECTOR (and the class) from connector.py
  connector.py      # the BaseConnector subclass; ends with CONNECTOR = <YourClass>
  dataset.yaml      # the dataset card, read by metadata()
  requirements.txt  # optional; libs installed into the build's isolated env
  tests/            # fixture-based, offline
```

> The system finds connectors lazily, by dataset id. **There is no central registry to maintain.**

`discovery._module_name` maps the id: **org lowercased, leaf hyphens → underscores**. So `physionet/ecg-qa-cot` → `...datasets.physionet.ecg_qa_cot/`. `connector_dir()` is deliberately import-free (uses `find_spec`) and requires a `dataset.yaml` to be present, which is how an org namespace package is distinguished from a real connector.

### A.4.3 Reusable bases

**`BaseHuggingFaceConnector`** (`bases/huggingface.py`) — you implement **only** `convert`:

```python
class BaseHuggingFaceConnector(BaseConnector[dict[str, Any]], ABC):
    HF_REPO: ClassVar[str]
    PARQUET_REVISION: ClassVar[str] = "refs/convert/parquet"
    def download(self, cache_dir: Path) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:  # inherited: one dict per row
```

It reads the Hub's **auto-converted parquet branch**, so any source format (CSV/JSON/…) is handled uniformly, without depending on `datasets`. `HF_TOKEN` is read from the env for gated repos. Fully private repos have no auto-parquet ref and are **not supported**.

**`BasePhysioNetConnector`** (`bases/physionet.py`) — you implement `download` + `convert`:

```python
class WfdbHeader(NamedTuple):

    dat_names: tuple[str, ...]; formats: tuple[str, ...]
    gains: tuple[float, ...]; baselines: tuple[int, ...]; direct_read: bool

@staticmethod
def _read_header(record_base: Path) -> WfdbHeader: ...
def _lead_loader(self, record_base: Path, header: WfdbHeader, lead_idx: int) -> Callable[[], pa.Array]: ...
```

### A.4.4 A full worked custom connector (the reference, verbatim)

`packages/timenet-connectors/src/timenet_connectors/datasets/chengsenwang/tsqa/connector.py` — this is the whole file, minus docstrings:

```python
import json
from typing import Any

from timenet.dataset import TimeFDataset, TimeSeries
from timenet.dataset.axis import OrdinalAxis
from timenet.types import Annotation, AnswerTask, TimeSeriesSpec, ureg
from timenet_connectors.bases.huggingface import BaseHuggingFaceConnector


_SPEC = TimeSeriesSpec(
    spec_type="tsqa_series",
    name="TSQA Series",
    unit_value=ureg.dimensionless,
)


class TSQAConnector(BaseHuggingFaceConnector):
    HF_REPO = "ChengsenWang/TSQA"

    def convert(self, raw_refs: list[dict[str, Any]]) -> TimeFDataset:
        dataset = TimeFDataset(metadata=self.metadata())
        for index, row in enumerate(raw_refs):
            series = json.loads(row["Series"])
            signals = series if series and isinstance(series[0], list) else [series]
            time_series = tuple(
                TimeSeries.from_values(
                    values,
                    spec=_SPEC,
                    signal=f"c{signal}",
                    time_axis=OrdinalAxis(),
                    time_series_id=f"row-{index}-c{signal}",
                )
                for signal, values in enumerate(signals)
            )
            record = dataset.add_record(time_series=time_series, record_id=f"row-{index}")
            record.add_annotation(Annotation(key="task", value=row["Task"], id=f"task-{index}"))
            if row.get("Label"):
                record.add_annotation(Annotation(key="label", value=row["Label"], id=f"label-{index}"))
            dataset.add_task(record, AnswerTask(prompt=row["Question"], target=row["Answer"], id=f"qa-{index}"))
        return dataset


CONNECTOR = TSQAConnector
```

`__init__.py`:
```python
from timenet_connectors.datasets.chengsenwang.tsqa.connector import (
    CONNECTOR as CONNECTOR,
    TSQAConnector as TSQAConnector,
)
```
`requirements.txt`:
```text

huggingface_hub>=0.24
```

### Validation — yes, extensively, at multiple layers

1. **Card**: JSON Schema (Draft 2020-12) via `jsonschema`, `additionalProperties: false`, errors aggregated into one `TimeNetInvalidCardError` message.
2. **Type construction**: every dataclass `__post_init__` validates — dtype in the supported set, enum categories non-empty/unique/strings, `value_shape` positive ints, `dimension_names` unique and matching length, spec_type not reserved, units resolvable against the shared pint registry, `n_values` a positive int, `signal` non-empty, `period_us` a `Fraction` ≥ 1 and int64-safe, interval `end > start`, `start >= 0`.
3. **`add_task`** runs a batch of checks: exactly-one-answer, annotation ids resolvable, record ids registered, time-series ids present on the target records, **span-vs-axis frame fit**, **span-within-window**, and `from_tasks` cycle detection.
4. **Span containment rule** (`record.py:check_span_within_window`), three cases: scoped → must lie in the **intersection** of the named series' windows; unscoped with a declared `time_span` → checked against that (lets an event land in a sensor gap on purpose); unscoped without → the **union** of timed series windows, "so that a convex hull of the series never masks a hole in the data."
5. **Integrity**: sha256 per file in the manifest.

## A.6 Signals / metadata / annotations — how they link

Six logical ids cross-reference everything: `record_id`, `time_series_id`, `annotation_id`, `task_id`, `source_id`, `subject_id`.

- **Signals** → `TimeSeries` attached to a `Record` via `add_record(time_series=(...))`. Typed by a shared `TimeSeriesSpec`. Values are lazy Arrow, stored in the values plane, joined via `time_series_index`.
- **Metadata (static attributes)** → `Annotation` with **no span**. There is deliberately no metadata field on `Record`. "The fact travels with every window drawn later from the record."
- **Annotations (labels/events/text)** → `Annotation` with `TimePoint` or `TimeInterval` span, optionally scoped to `time_series_ids`. A single event can span several sensors: "The shared timing indicates one physical process, not a per-signal artifact."
- **Targets** → `Task`, referencing records by `record_ids`, context by `input_annotation_ids`, and answers either inline (`target`) or by reference (`target_annotation_ids`).

Value-deduped annotations are the pattern for shared per-question metadata — see the ECG connector's `_qtype_id`/`_template_ann_id`/`_options_id`/`_context_id` helpers plus `dataset.register_annotations(...)`.

## A.7 The TimeNet → OpenTSLM handoff: **there is no bridge. This is the gap.**

What actually exists:

**(a) `TimeFTorchDataset`** (`packages/timenet/src/timenet/torch.py`) — the only ML-facing surface. `__getitem__` returns:

```python
{
    "record_id":    str,
    "series":       tuple[Tensor, ...],   # each (n_steps, *value_shape), original dtype
    "series_masks": tuple[Tensor, ...],   # bool, True where present; all-True if non-nullable
    "tasks":        tuple[Task, ...],     # Python objects, NOT tensors
    "annotations":  tuple[Annotation, ...],
}
```
plus an optional `transform`. String-dtype series raise; enum series come back as int64 category codes. The docs are explicit that you supply the glue:

> To feed a `DataLoader`, select the fields that your model needs. Use a `transform` on the dataset, or a `collate_fn` on the loader… Series lengths also vary between records.

**(b) The ECG-QA-CoT connector goes the *other* direction** — it ingests OpenTSLM's release. From `datasets/physionet/ecg_qa_cot/connector.py`:

```python
# Precomputed CoT rows (question, answer, rationale, template). OpenTSLM's release is the only
# public source. This is a swappable constant so a mirror can replace it.
ECG_QA_COT_URL = "https://polybox.ethz.ch/index.php/s/D5QaJSEw4dXkzXm/download/ecg_qa_cot_final.zip"
```

**(c) The only "handoff spec" is prose in two dataset cards.** From `datasets/physionet/ecg_qa_cot/dataset.yaml`:

```yaml
# Training convention: each record carries an AnswerTask whose `target` is the short evaluation
# label and whose `rationale` is the chain-of-thought target to fine-tune on. The multiple-choice
# candidates are stored as the `answer_options` annotation. Signals are archival raw (12 leads,
# 500 Hz, millivolt); reproduce OpenTSLM's training preprocessing (downsample to 100 Hz, per-lead
# z-normalize) at load time.
```

And `datasets/physionet/sleep_edfx/dataset.yaml`:

```yaml
# Training convention: the target of each ClassificationTask is the label the scorer wrote, so
# `Sleep stage 4` stays `Sleep stage 4`. The 5-class problem most papers report merges stage 3
# with stage 4 into N3 and drops the epochs labeled `Movement time` or `Sleep stage ?`. Signals
# are archival raw (every signal at the rate and in the unit its own EDF header states, no
# resampling); a recording can span about a day, so trim it to the scored sleep at load time.
```

**Design principle to internalize:** TimeNet stores **archival raw** signals — no resampling, no normalization, native units. All of OpenTSLM's preprocessing (100 Hz downsample, z-score, 30 s windowing, patch padding) is expected to happen **at load time, in the adapter you write**. That adapter is the missing piece and is exactly the "reusable ingestion pipeline" the challenge asks for.

## A.8 Splits, irregular sampling, missing values, variable length

- **Splits**: no first-class split concept. The convention is a **static annotation**: `Annotation(key="split", value="train"|"validation"|"test", id=f"...-split")` — see the ECG connector, `record.add_annotations([Annotation(key="split", value=split, id=f"ptbxl-{ecg_id}-split")])`. Note it groups by recording (`split_of_ecg.setdefault(...)`), which is the leakage-control mechanism: every question about one ECG lands in the same split. There is no automated leakage checker.
- **Irregular sampling**: first-class — `IrregularAxis` + a required `time_offsets_loader` giving one int64 µs offset per value. Constructing an `IrregularAxis` series without it raises; attaching one to a non-irregular axis also raises ("which already determines every time offset").
- **Missing values**: `spec.nullable=True` + Arrow validity bits. `to_numpy()` **raises** `TimeFValidationError` if nulls are present; use `to_arrow()` (keeps nulls exactly) or `to_numpy_and_mask() -> (values, present)`. "The values array holds zero, false, or an empty string at each missing position. That placeholder is not an observation. The mask carries that information."
- **Variable length**: native — `n_values` is per-series, chunking is per-series, and the format has no padding concept. Padding is the consumer's job (`collate_fn`).
- **Units**: pint, on the spec, part of the type. `from timenet.types import ureg`; the registry defines extras like `bpm`. Specs pickle units **by name** so multiprocessing DataLoaders work.
- **Timezones**: only via `Record.start_time` (tz-aware datetime or Unix µs). Absent is a supported state.

## B.2 The two architectures

### OpenTSLM-SP (Soft Prompt) — `src/opentslm/model/llm/OpenTSLMSP.py`

- **Encoder**: `TransformerCNNEncoder` — `nn.Conv1d(1, 128, kernel_size=4, stride=4, bias=False)` patch embedding → learnable `pos_embed` `(1, 1024, 128)` → LayerNorm+Dropout → `nn.TransformerEncoder` of **6 layers, 8 heads, ff_dim=1024, GELU, batch_first**. Input `[B, L]` → output `[B, L/4, 128]`.
- **Projector**: `MLPProjector` = `LayerNorm(128) → Linear(128, hidden_size) → GELU → Dropout(0.0)`.
- **Fusion**: the projected patch embeddings are **spliced directly into the LLM's `inputs_embeds` sequence**, interleaved between the tokenized text chunks. The LLM backbone is **frozen** (`for p in self.llm.parameters(): p.requires_grad = False`); only encoder + projector (+ optional LoRA) train.
- The interleaving happens in `pad_and_apply_batch` (the docstring calls itself "probably the most crucial part of OpenTSLM-SP"): order is `pre_prompt` → for each i: `time_series_text[i]` then `ts_proj[i]` → `post_prompt`.
- **Loss**: answer embeddings are concatenated after the prompt; `labels` are `-100` everywhere except the answer span.
- **LoRA**: `enable_lora(lora_r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.0, target_modules=[q,k,v,o,gate,up,down]_proj)`.
- **Checkpoint**: `{"encoder_state", "projector_state", "lora_enabled", "lora_state"?}` — tiny.

### OpenTSLM-Flamingo (cross-attention) — `src/opentslm/model/llm/OpenTSLMFlamingo.py`

- **Encoder**: `CNNTokenizer` — the *same* Conv1d patch embed + pos_embed + LayerNorm/Dropout, **without** the transformer stack.
- **Fusion**: real `open_flamingo`. The LM is extended in place (`extend_instance(lang_encoder, FlamingoLMMixin)`), gated cross-attention layers are inserted every `cross_attn_every_n_layers` (=1), and a Perceiver resampler sits between the encoder and the cross-attn.
- The `<image>` and `<|endofchunk|>` special tokens are added to the tokenizer, and the prompt is built as a literal string:
  ```python
  prompt_text = item["pre_prompt"]
  for ts_text in item["time_series_text"]:
      prompt_text += f" {tokenizer.decode([media_token_id])} {ts_text} {tokenizer.decode([endofchunk_token_id])}"
  if item["post_prompt"]:
      prompt_text += f" {item['post_prompt']}"
  ```
- **Trainable**: everything frozen, then `model.perceiver`, `model.lang_encoder.gated_cross_attn_layers`, LM input embeddings (unless `freeze_lm_embeddings`), and `model.vision_encoder` are unfrozen. `TimeSeriesFlamingoWithTrainableEncoder` overrides `_encode_vision_x` precisely because "In the original Flamingo, the vision_encoder is a CLIPModel, which is not trainable (with torch.no_grad()). Here, we use a TimeSeriesCNNEncoder, which is trainable."
- **Checkpoint**: `{"llm": full state_dict}` — large.

### Base LLMs

Factory `OpenTSLM.load_pretrained(repo_id, device=None, cache_dir=None, enable_lora=False)` dispatches on the repo-id suffix (`-sp` → `OpenTSLMSP`, `-flamingo` → `OpenTSLMFlamingo`) and maps the prefix to a base LLM:

| repo prefix | base LLM |
| --- | --- |
| `llama-3.2-3b` | `meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B` |
| `llama-3.2-1b` | `meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B` (default) |
| `gemma-3-1b` | `google/gemma-3-1b` |
| `gemma-3-270m` | `google/gemma-3-270m` |

Flamingo's `_infer_decoder_layers_attr_name` also knows `opt, gptj, pythia, mpt, mosaicgpt, gemma, gemma2, gemma3, medgemma`, with special handling: `Gemma3ForConditionalGeneration` → `language_model.layers`, else `model.layers`.

## B.3 THE DATA FORMAT (the priority section)

### B.3.1 The exact training-example dict

`QADataset._format_sample` calls `PromptWithAnswer(...).to_dict()`. From `src/opentslm/prompt/prompt_with_answer.py`:

```python
def to_dict(self):
    return {
        "answer": self.answer,
        "post_prompt": self.post_prompt.get_text(),
        "pre_prompt": self.pre_prompt.get_text(),
        "time_series": self.text_time_series_prompt_time_series,
        "time_series_text": self.text_time_series_prompt_texts,
    }
```

**Exactly five keys.** That is the complete contract.

| Key | Type before collate | Type after collate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `pre_prompt` | `str` | unchanged |
| `time_series_text` | `List[str]`, one per series | unchanged |
| `time_series` | `List[np.ndarray]`, each **1-D** | `torch.Tensor` `(num_series, padded_len)` |
| `post_prompt` | `str` | unchanged |
| `answer` | `str`, already EOS-suffixed | unchanged |

`FullPrompt.to_dict()` is identical minus `answer` (inference path).

### B.3.2 The construction code, verbatim

`src/opentslm/time_series_datasets/QADataset.py`:

```python
def _format_sample(self, row):
    answer = self._get_answer(row)
    if not answer.endswith(self.EOS_TOKEN):
        answer += self.EOS_TOKEN

    return PromptWithAnswer(
        TextPrompt(self._get_pre_prompt(row).strip()),
        self._get_text_time_series_prompt_list(row),
        TextPrompt(self._get_post_prompt(row).strip()),
        answer.strip(),
    ).to_dict()
```

Note: pre/post are `.strip()`ped, the answer gets the EOS token appended **before** stripping.

### B.3.3 The time-series field — hard constraints

`src/opentslm/prompt/text_time_series_prompt.py`:

```python
class TextTimeSeriesPrompt(Prompt):
    def __init__(self, text: str, time_series: Sequence):
        assert isinstance(text, str), "Text must be a string!"
        assert isinstance(time_series, (np.ndarray, Sequence)), \
            "Time series must be a list or numpy array!"

        ts_array = np.array(time_series)

        assert ts_array.ndim == 1, "Time series must be one-dimensional! You can input multiple time series, but each time series must be a one-dimensional array."
        assert ts_array.size > 0, "Time series must not be empty!"
        assert np.issubdtype(ts_array.dtype, np.number), \
            "Time series must contain only numeric values!"
```

So: **strictly 1-D, non-empty, numeric.** Multivariate is expressed as *N separate `TextTimeSeriesPrompt` objects*, each with its own caption text — never as a 2-D array.

### B.3.4 Multiple series per sample

Pass a list of `TextTimeSeriesPrompt` from `_get_text_time_series_prompt_list`. `FullPrompt`/`PromptWithAnswer` unzip it into two parallel lists:

```python
self.text_time_series_prompt_texts = list(map(lambda x: x.get_text(), text_time_series_prompt_list))
self.text_time_series_prompt_time_series = list(map(lambda x: x.get_time_series(), text_time_series_prompt_list))
```

**The two lists are positionally aligned.** `time_series_text[i]` captions `time_series[i]`. Counts in the shipped datasets: TSQA 1, M4 1, Sleep 1, HAR 3, ECG-QA **12** (one per lead), PAMAP2 varies.

### B.3.5 Normalization — always in the dataset, **not** in the collate fn

Every shipped dataset z-scores per series inside `_get_text_time_series_prompt_list`, and **writes the pre-normalization mean and std into the caption text**. This is the single most distinctive convention in the codebase.

TSQA (`TSQADataset.py`):
```python

stds = series.std(dim=0, keepdim=True)
series = (series - means) / (stds + 1e-8)
mean_val = means.flatten()[0].item()
std_val = stds.flatten()[0].item()
return [TextTimeSeriesPrompt(
    f"This is the time series, it has mean {mean_val:.4f} and std {std_val:.4f}.",
    series.tolist())]
```

```python
stds  = series.std(dim=1, keepdim=True)
min_std = 1e-6
stds = torch.clamp(stds, min=min_std)
series_norm = (series - means) / stds
...

```
